findings.claim: Conflict-gate OPA invocation omits scp_common.rego, disabling the waiver-aware and rule-config layers during conflict-gate evaluation
findings.evidence: tests/conflict_gate/test_conflict_gate.py:62-87, function _run_opa: `cmd = [opa, 'eval', '--format=json', '--data', str(rule_path), '--input', str(fixture_input_path), 'data.main.deny']`. Only the individual rule file (e.g. policies/SCP-R-001.rego) is passed via --data. policies/scp_common.rego is not loaded. Without it, scp_active_waiver_for, scp_waivers, scp_rule_config_disabled, scp_rule_config_entry, scp_dateish_ns are all undefined. Through NAF, `not scp_active_waiver_for(...)` and `not scp_rule_config_disabled(...)` are always true, so the deny rule fires on all raw findings regardless of any waiver or rule-config state. The conflict-gate cannot detect Rego/Python disagreements in waiver-suppressed or rule-config-disabled code paths.
findings.impact: AC 020C.1(iv) requires the CI job to assert rego.verdict == python.verdict == expected.verdict. A waiver-suppressed fixture where Rego correctly suppresses (allow) but Python produces deny (or vice versa) would not be detected. The conflict-gate's authority over the waiver-aware code path is therefore not tested. If scp_common.rego develops a waiver logic bug, the conflict-gate will not catch it. The fixture corpus (2 per rule) represents only the no-waiver code paths.
findings.mitigation: Update _run_opa to also pass `--data` for scp_common.rego: `COMMON = POLICIES_DIR / 'scp_common.rego'`; add `'--data', str(COMMON)` to cmd. Add at least one waiver-suppressed fixture per rule: `fixtures/SCP-R-001/waived/input.yml` (valid waiver in data.waivers) + `expected-verdict.json` (verdict: allow). Confirm OPA correctly returns allow and Python also returns allow (or skips gracefully). AC §9.4 requires ≥6 fixtures total (2 per rule); adding waived scenarios would also raise fixture coverage.

findings.claim: waivers_applied[*].expires_at in policy-check-summary.schema.json requires date-only format but the system produces date-time values, causing schema validation failure for adopters using date-time waivers
findings.evidence: schemas/policy-check-summary.schema.json lines 128-133: expires_at property has `"pattern": "^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}$", "format": "date"` (date-only). By contrast, schemas/waiver.schema.json and schemas/waivers-file.schema.json both define `dateOrDateTime` allowing either format. The warn rules in all three Rego files emit `"expires_at": object.get(w, "expires_at", "")` verbatim from the waiver. lib/policy_check_invocation.sh Python processor writes `entry["expires_at"] = str(warning.get("expires_at", ""))` verbatim. Test scp_r_001_test.rego:129 uses `"expires_at": "2099-12-31T23:59:59Z"` (date-time). A waiver with this value produces a waivers-applied.json entry with `"expires_at": "2099-12-31T23:59:59Z"` which fails the `^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}$` pattern constraint at the Validate policy-check summary schema step. The same applies to disabled_rules[*].expires_at (same date-only pattern) when rule-config uses date-time expires_at.
findings.impact: Any adopter repo whose waivers.json or .scp/rule-config.yaml uses date-time format for expires_at (which is explicitly allowed by the waiver and rule-config schemas) will fail CI at the summary validation step. The adopt-side schema (waiver.schema.json, rule-config.schema.json) and the output-side schema (policy-check-summary.schema.json) are inconsistent. This is a silent incompatibility that would surface only at runtime on a waiver-suppressed PR.
findings.mitigation: Either (a) extend waivers_applied[*].expires_at and disabled_rules[*].expires_at in policy-check-summary.schema.json to use the same dateOrDateTime anyOf constraint as the waiver and rule-config schemas; or (b) normalize the expires_at field to date-only in the Python processor in lib/policy_check_invocation.sh by truncating at the T boundary. Option (a) is the cleaner fix since it avoids lossy normalization.

findings.claim: CODEOWNERS does not cover schemas/rule-config.schema.json; the AC explicitly requires CODEOWNERS coverage for this file
findings.evidence: CODEOWNERS file (1 line): `policies/** @jrnb2024`. This covers policies/scp_common.rego (correct). schemas/rule-config.schema.json is NOT under any CODEOWNERS rule. The review instruction AC states: 'CODEOWNERS coverage for scp_common.rego + rule-config.schema.json'. WP-SCP-020 §4 020K defines CODEOWNERS coverage requirements. schemas/rule-config.schema.json controls which rules can be disabled by callers and what expiry format is accepted — a security-sensitive file. Also uncovered: schemas/policy-check-summary.schema.json, schemas/waiver.schema.json, schemas/waivers-file.schema.json, .github/workflows/policy-check.yml, lib/policy_check_invocation.sh, tests/conflict_gate/.
findings.impact: Any PR can modify schemas/rule-config.schema.json without @jrnb2024 review, weakening or removing the `additionalProperties: false` constraint, changing required fields, or expanding the pattern to allow arbitrary rule IDs. This is a governance bypass path. Per the review AC this is explicitly a missing deliverable for slice 020C.1.
findings.mitigation: Extend CODEOWNERS with at minimum: `schemas/** @jrnb2024` and `lib/** @jrnb2024` and `.github/workflows/** @jrnb2024` and `tests/conflict_gate/** @jrnb2024`. Minimum required by AC: add `schemas/rule-config.schema.json @jrnb2024` or the broader `schemas/**` pattern.

findings.claim: Conflict-gate CI job downloads and executes an OPA binary with no SHA256 verification and no Sigstore attestation, creating a supply-chain gap relative to the policy-check workflow standard
findings.evidence: .github/workflows/conflict-gate.yml lines 42-48: `OPA_VERSION="v0.69.0"`, `OPA_URL="https://openpolicyagent.org/downloads/${OPA_VERSION}/opa_linux_amd64"`, `curl -fsSL "$OPA_URL" -o /tmp/opa`. No SHA256 comparison step. No `gh attestation verify` step. By contrast, policy-check.yml implements: lockfile-pinned version, SHA256 verification via verify_sha256(), and Sigstore attestation via `gh attestation verify`. The two workflows also use different OPA versions (conflict-gate hardcodes v0.69.0; policy-check uses the version from scripts/.tool-versions), creating an OPA version divergence risk where the same Rego evaluates differently under each workflow.
findings.impact: The conflict-gate job accepts an unverified binary from the network on every run. A MITM or compromised CDN could inject a modified OPA binary that either suppresses deny findings or falsifies agreement. WP-SCP-020 §8 explicitly lists supply-chain as a high-priority risk, and 020B(v) mandates version-pinned + SHA256-verified + Sigstore-attested binaries. The conflict-gate job is in scope for this standard and is currently non-conformant. OPA version drift between workflows also means a rule may behave differently in the two CI contexts, undermining the value of the conflict-gate.
findings.mitigation: Align conflict-gate.yml with policy-check.yml: read OPA version from scripts/.tool-versions, read SHA256 from scripts/scp-policy-check.lock, verify after download, run `gh attestation verify`. Alternatively, extract OPA installation into a shared composite action so both workflows use a single verified installation path.

findings.claim: statuses: write permission was added to policy-check.yml without a formal spec amendment to WP-SCP-020 §4 020B(iii), creating spec-vs-impl drift
findings.evidence: policy-check.yml lines 42-44: `permissions: contents: read; statuses: write`. WP-SCP-020-policy-federation-primitive.md §4 020B(iii): 'permissions: = contents: read (verified sufficient). No id-token, no checks: write, no pull-requests: write.' The original spec was written before 020C.1(vi) required a commit-status post step. The plan document still reads `contents: read` as the complete permissions block. No D-NNN decision record acknowledges this change; docs/DECISIONS.md not updated; the plan doc §4 020B(iii) still says `contents: read`.
findings.impact: Adopters reading the plan spec to understand the privilege footprint of the reusable workflow will see `contents: read` and not expect `statuses: write`. ADOPT-001 §12 adopter guidance (020H part 3, not yet written) must reflect the accurate permissions. Spec drift compounds over time as additional sub-slices add further permission requirements. Minor security surface increase: statuses:write allows the workflow to post arbitrary commit statuses on behalf of the caller's GITHUB_TOKEN, which could be abused to spoof CI signals if the workflow is compromised.
findings.mitigation: Add a D-NNN row to docs/DECISIONS.md ratifying the statuses:write addition and amend WP-SCP-020 §4 020B(iii) to read `permissions: contents: read, statuses: write` with a cross-reference to 020C.1(vi) as the source. Update ADOPT-001 §12 adopter guidance to reflect the correct permissions block when 020H part 3 is authored.

findings.claim: ADOPT-001 project-onboarding document does not reference the .scp/rule-config.yaml caller-side artefact introduced in slice 020C.1(v)
findings.evidence: grep for 'rule-config' OR 'rule_config' in docs/adoption/ADOPT-001-project-onboarding.md returns zero matches. The review AC explicitly states: 'the ADOPT-001 doc references the new caller-side artefact (.scp/rule-config.yaml) — if not, flag as a missing follow-up.' WP-SCP-020 §4 020C.1(v) defines the caller-side rule-config override as a v1.0.0 deliverable. Without documentation in ADOPT-001, adopters have no guidance on: (a) the .scp/rule-config.yaml schema, (b) the disable/justification/expires_at required keys, (c) the one-release warning grace period for expired rule-config overrides, (d) how to invoke the override without breaking the schema validation step.
findings.impact: Adopters cannot use the rule-config override feature correctly. Governance: the rule-config mechanism is a power-user escape hatch with intentional friction (schema-validated, expires_at required, one-release warning). Without documentation, adopters bypass friction through trial-and-error, undermining the governance intent. Per §4.3 fixpoint criteria this is a missing deliverable for the slice.
findings.mitigation: Add a '## Caller-side rule override (.scp/rule-config.yaml)' section to ADOPT-001 covering: schema location, required fields, the `disable: true + justification + expires_at` pattern, the expired-disable one-release grace period and warning annotation, and the link to schemas/rule-config.schema.json. This is explicitly a pre-020H part 3 deliverable (020H part 3 covers §12 adoption appendix; this section belongs there or as a §11 addendum).

findings.claim: policies/README.md rule template still shows the pre-020C.1 deny pattern without the waiver-aware _raw_findings split, silently teaching future rule authors to produce non-conformant rules
findings.evidence: policies/README.md Rule Template section (lines 19-27): the deny rule template is `deny contains { message, rule_id, ... } if { violating_condition }`. This is the pre-020C.1 shape. All three implemented rules now use the `_raw_findings` intermediate set + `not scp_active_waiver_for(...)` + `not scp_rule_config_disabled(...)` guards (see SCP-R-001.rego:30-98, SCP-R-002.rego:25-109, SCP-R-003.rego:21-38). The checklist step 5 mentions conflict-gate fixtures but not the waiver/rule-config integration contract. Rule RFC process (020H.1) is not yet delivered but the README is already in use.
findings.impact: The next rule added (rule 4+, post-RFC) by a new contributor following the README template would produce a non-waiver-aware rule that bypasses all suppression logic. The gap would not be caught by the coverage gate (opa test) unless the coverage tests happen to include waiver and rule-config tests as well. Silent regression path for governance weakening.
findings.mitigation: Update the Rule Template section to reflect the 020C.1 waiver-aware pattern: show `_raw_findings` intermediate set, `deny` guarded by `not scp_active_waiver_for(...)` and `not scp_rule_config_disabled(...)`, and `warn` rules for observability. Add a checklist item between steps 4 and 5: 'Factor deny logic through <rule>_raw_findings and guard the public deny rule with scp_active_waiver_for + scp_rule_config_disabled per the 020C.1 pattern in any existing rule.'

findings.claim: Post policy-check read-back commit status hardcodes 3 as the total rule count, producing incorrect enabled_count for all future rule library sizes
findings.evidence: policy-check.yml Build policy-check summary + Post policy-check read-back commit status step (line ~942): `enabled_count = max(0, 3 - len(rule_ids))`. The number 3 is hardcoded. Additionally, disabled_rules includes the SCP-R-003 no-manifest-applicable observability record (reason='no-manifest-applicable') which gets included in rule_ids when computing enabled_count, so a run with no manifests would report 2 rules enabled, 1 disabled (SCP-R-003) even though all three rules are functionally active.
findings.impact: When the rule library grows to 4+ rules (post-020H.1 RFC), every PR will display 'X rules enabled' where X is wrong. The SCP-R-003 no-manifest case already produces misleading output: repos with no manifests in the changed set see '2 rules enabled, 1 disabled: SCP-R-003 until 2099-12-31 (no-manifest-applicable)' which misrepresents SCP-R-003 as 'disabled' rather than 'not applicable'. WP-SCP-023 aggregation will inherit this inaccuracy.
findings.mitigation: Replace the hardcoded count with a dynamic derivation: read the total rule count from the policy bundle (e.g., count .rego files matching SCP-R-NNN.rego) or maintain a version-manifest.json that declares the active rule count. Separately, filter the SCP-R-003 no-manifest-applicable entries out of the disabled_rules count when computing enabled_count (or emit them under a separate 'not_applicable' field in the summary schema).

findings.claim: scp_r_002_is_waiver_payload has a redundant second rule for empty arrays that never produces additional behaviour
findings.evidence: policies/SCP-R-002.rego lines 145-153: two rules for scp_r_002_is_waiver_payload — one guards on `count(input) > 0`, the second on `count(input) == 0`. Together they are logically equivalent to `is_array(input)`. The per-entry raw_findings rules use `some index, entry in input` which produces nothing for an empty array regardless of scp_r_002_is_waiver_payload's value. The second rule is therefore a no-op. The comment at line 141-143 says 'Empty array remains a no-op' which is correct, but the second rule suggests the author believed it was needed to achieve that no-op semantics.
findings.impact: No correctness impact. Future maintainers may believe removing the second rule would change behaviour (it would not). Adds cognitive load when reading the logic.
findings.mitigation: Remove the second scp_r_002_is_waiver_payload rule (lines 150-153). Add an inline comment on the remaining rule: '# empty array: scp_r_002_is_waiver_payload is false, so per-entry rules below cannot fire.' This is a cosmetic fix; acceptable to defer to the next pass.
